name: Vute (Babute)
overview: A people of great warriors who came from Adamawa, the Vute (Babute) conquered their lands by crossing the Sanaga near Mbandjock, and today neighbour the Eton, the Mbamois, the Nanga, the Yezoum and the Mvele. Hereditary chiefdom, hunting, fishing and farming, cassava couscous and the war dance with the djiiŋ drum characterise them.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: The group lives alongside the Eton, the Mbamois, the Nanga, the Yezoum and the Mvele, without speaking their languages.
Vute is also spoken in Mbam-et-Kim, Djérem (Adamawa) and as far as Sudan.
Formerly, people married among the Babute; today, mostly with other peoples.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Vute settled at the end of military conquests, with no religious value attached to the place.
First settled on the other bank of the Sanaga, near Mbandjock, they are said to have come from Adamawa, where some Vute still live.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: The chief (tá), guarantor of the community, owns all the land; the chiefdom is hereditary and passes to one of the sons of the deceased.
The chief decides with his notables, and conflicts are settled at the chiefdom.
A democratic community, but the unmarried man, with no land or home, counts for little.
Any clan can inherit, but only boys were favoured; plotting against the chief drew, it was believed, the deadly wrath of the ancestors.
Formerly, the wife knelt to address her husband; children owe great respect to their elders.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family.
The boy became a man after a three-month retreat in the bush for circumcision, at around 16-17; he could then marry.
Steps: marriage proposal, long engagement (five to six years in the past) to prepare the two spouses, then bride price.
Bride price: machete and hoe (to check that the suitor will know how to cultivate and feed his wife), file, a little money.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Graves are cleaned in December.
Birth is a joy, formerly celebrated; death takes one back to the forebears.
The enthronement of the chief is a taboo subject.

The snake is the great food taboo of the Vute, a distinctive feature among their neighbours; pregnant women avoid tortoise and four-legged animals; fishermen and hunters abstain from relations during the day.
Incest is the capital offence: it requires purification rites and can bring a curse on two families.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: hunting, fishing, a little farming. Women: mainly farming and fishing.
The chief owns the land.
Ancestral crafts: baskets, carrying baskets, raphia plates (trə́ə́) for serving couscous.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Old clothing: the mbinti loincloth, for everyone.
Traditional medicine is disappearing for lack of transmission: people turn to the knowledge of other groups.
Beauty: the very robust and strong man; the tattooed woman, a good cook, adorned with beads around the waist.
Courtship: the hard-working man who offers presents to his future mother-in-law; the woman a good cook.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: The djiiŋ drum accompanies the war dance of victories; the makongo, a kind of lamellophone piano, sets the rhythm of traditional ceremonies.
Festivals are mostly funerary.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Great warriors, the Vute settled after winning the war and crossing the Sanaga.

sections.title: The names
items: Names specific to each sex, always meaningful; no names specific to twins.
The parents asked their own parents which name to give, often that of a departed relative; the name does not change.
Pseudonym: məsə; appellative -yo (Mve-yo).
The founding ancestor, Mvɛn-baa, is “the prince”.

lessons.title: Who are the Vute (Babute)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Vute (Babute) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Vute (Babute) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Vute (Babute) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Vute (Babute) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Vute (Babute) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Vute (Babute) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The group lives alongside the Eton, the Mbamois, the Nanga, the Yezoum and the Mvele, without speaking their languages. • Vute is also spoken in Mbam-et-Kim, in Djérem (Adamawa) and as far as Sudan. • In the past, people married among the Babute; today, mostly with other peoples. • The Vute settled at the end of military conquests, with no religious value attached to the place. • First established on the other bank of the Sanaga, near Mbandjock, they are said to have come from Adamawa, where some Vute still live.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A people of great warriors who came from Adamawa, the Vute (Babute) conquered their lands by crossing the Sanaga near Mbandjock, and today neighbour the Eton, the Mbamois, the Nanga, the Yezoum and the Mvele. Hereditary chiefdom, hunting, fishing and farming, cassava couscous and the war dance with the djiiŋ drum characterise them.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Vute (Babute) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Vute (Babute)

lessons.competence: Describe how the Vute (Babute) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Vute (Babute) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Vute (Babute) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The chief (tá), guarantor of the community, owns all the land; the chiefdom is hereditary and passes to one of the sons of the deceased. steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Vute (Babute)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Vute (Babute), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Vute (Babute).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Vute (Babute), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Vute (Babute).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: cassava couscous, pistachio dishes. • Drinks: maize beer (formerly). • Men: hunting, fishing, a little farming. Women: mainly farming and fishing.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Vute (Babute) eat mainly cassava couscous, groundnut dishes (pistachio). Traditional drinks: maize beer. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Vute (Babute): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Vute (Babute)
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth

vocabulary.frenchText: <the one who was born through difficulties>

lessons.competence: Explain how the Vute (Babute) welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Vute (Babute) family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Vute (Babute) welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Vute (Babute) family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Vute (Babute)
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments

steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

student.memo: Among the Vute (Babute), traditional dances (war dance with the djiiŋ, ceremonies) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: djiiŋ drum, lamellophone. Festival(s): funeral celebrations.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Vute (Babute)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Vute (Babute), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Vute (Babute). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Vute (Babute), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Vute (Babute). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: hunting, fishing, a little farming. Women: mostly farming and fishing. • The chief owns the lands. • Ancestral crafts: baskets, carrying baskets, raffia plates (trə́ə́) for serving couscous.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: hunting, fishing, a little farming. Women: mainly farming and fishing. The chief owns the land.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Vute (Babute)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover how the Vute (Babute) make a living from their work.

activities.title: I classify

activities.instruction: Explain how one obtains land to cultivate.

activities.title: I calculate
activities.instruction: Imagine the calendar of a working year (seasons, harvests, festivals).

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: hunting, fishing, a little farming. Women: mainly farming and fishing. The chief owns the land.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Vute (Babute)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Vute (Babute), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Vute (Babute). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Vute (Babute), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Vute (Babute). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Graves are cleaned in December. • Birth is a joy, formerly celebrated; death brings one back to the ancestors. • The enthronement of the chief is a taboo subject. • The snake is the great food taboo of the Vute, a singularity among their neighbours; the pregnant woman avoids tortoise and four-legged animals; fishermen and hunters abstain from relations by day. • Incest is the cardinal fault: it requires purification rites and may bring a curse on two families.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Graves are cleaned in December. Birth is a joy, formerly celebrated; death brings one back to the ancestors.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Vute (Babute) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Vute (Babute) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I show respect

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: Graves are cleaned in December. Birth is a joy, formerly celebrated; death brings one back to the ancestors.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Vute
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Vute (Babute) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Vute (Babute) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Vute (Babute) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Vute (Babute) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Vute. • Greetings: Odzəba = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Nidzəba = morning greeting (several people); Odzəya = morning greeting (as a sign of deference/respect). • Counting from 1 to 5: Mwi, Mbaa, Tarə, Nasə, Ngii. • The founding ancestor, Mvɛn-baa, is “the prince”. • Great warriors, the Vute settled after winning the war and crossing the Sanaga.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Vute are the first steps towards communicating with the Vute (Babute). Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Vute.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Vute are the first steps towards communicating with the Vute (Babute). Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
